items.prompt: Why does a stick insect stay so hard to spot on a branch?

options.label: Its shape and stillness together make it look like a twig
options.feedback: The narrow brown body already looks like part of the plant, and staying still is what keeps that resemblance from breaking.

options.label: It moves faster than any bird can track
options.feedback: Speed would only matter after it had already been noticed, and a spotted stick insect has already lost.

options.label: It sprays a strong scent that keeps predators away
options.feedback: Some insects do rely on smell, but a stick insect's defence is entirely visual, not chemical.

options.label: It buries itself in the bark each morning
options.feedback: It rests in the open on stems and leaves; there is no burying involved.

items.ok_line: Shape alone would not be enough without the stillness.
items.ko_line: Ask what a twig does, and does not do, all day.
items.exp_title: A shape that only works if nothing moves
items.exp_text: A stick insect's long, thin, mottled body already matches the color and outline of a dead twig. That likeness only holds up if the insect stays still, since any motion breaks the illusion no matter how good the shape is. So it freezes for long stretches, and when it must shift position at all, it sways slowly the way a twig sways in moving air.

items.prompt: How does a leaf insect avoid being noticed among real leaves?

options.label: Its flattened body copies a leaf's shape, veins, and even ragged edges
options.feedback: The wings and body are flattened and shaped like a leaf blade, with lines that mimic veins and edges that look chewed or browned.

options.label: It coats itself in real leaf fragments
options.feedback: Nothing is glued or gathered from outside; the resemblance is built into the insect's own body.

options.label: It changes shape to match whichever leaf it lands on
options.feedback: The shape is fixed from birth, not adjustable leaf by leaf.

options.label: It curls into a ball that looks like a seed
options.feedback: A leaf insect stays flat and spread out, the opposite of curling into a ball.

items.ok_line: A leaf shape imitated all the way down to its flaws.
items.ko_line: The resemblance is not just outline; it goes into the fine detail.
items.exp_text: A leaf insect's wings are flattened and broadened into the shape of a leaf blade, with raised lines running across them like veins. Some even show patches that look like browning or edges that look nibbled, details that make the copy closer than a plain green outline would. A predator searching for a shape that stands out from the leaves around it finds nothing to catch its eye.

items.prompt: Why do some insects wear bright colors like red, yellow, or orange with black?

options.label: The colors warn predators that they sting, bite, or taste terrible
options.feedback: Predators learn fast that this pattern means trouble and avoid it after one bad experience.

options.label: Bright colors help them find mates faster
options.feedback: Some patterns do help mates recognize each other, but the sharp red-yellow-black combination specifically signals danger to predators, not partners.

options.label: Bright colors reflect heat and keep them cool
options.feedback: Color has no meaningful effect on how much heat a small insect's body gains or loses here.

options.label: Bright colors are simply left over from earlier body patterns
options.feedback: Nothing about these patterns is accidental; they show up again and again across unrelated insects precisely because they work.

items.ok_line: Loud colors are a warning label, not decoration.
items.ko_line: These insects are not trying to disappear; they are trying to be seen and remembered.
items.exp_title: A warning label worn on the body
items.exp_text: An insect that can sting, spray acid, or taste foul gains nothing from hiding, because being eaten even once is fatal. Instead it displays a bold, high-contrast pattern that a predator can learn and remember after a single bad encounter. Once learned, that same pattern makes the predator turn away the next time, before it ever attacks.

items.prompt: Why does a harmless hoverfly have yellow and black stripes like a wasp?

options.label: Copying a wasp's warning pattern makes predators avoid it too, even though it has no sting
options.feedback: A bird that has already learned to avoid stinging wasps avoids the hoverfly too, without ever testing whether it can sting.

options.label: The stripes help it blend into flower petals
options.feedback: Bold black and yellow stripes stand out against petals rather than blending with them.

options.label: It needs the pattern to attract other hoverflies
options.feedback: Mates recognize hoverflies by scent and behavior, not by matching a wasp's coloring.

options.label: The stripes absorb sunlight for extra energy
options.feedback: Stripe color has nothing to do with gathering warmth; the pattern's only job is to be recognized.

items.ko_title: It has no sting to advertise
items.ko_line: The hoverfly gains nothing from its own defences, because it has none. Whose defences is it using instead?
items.exp_text: A hoverfly cannot sting, but it wears the same black and yellow pattern that a wasp uses to warn predators away. A bird that has already been stung once, or has watched another bird react to that pattern, avoids anything marked the same way afterward. The hoverfly survives on a reputation it never earned, borrowed entirely from an insect it merely resembles.

items.prompt: Why do some jumping spiders walk on six legs and wave their front legs like antennae?

options.label: They imitate ants, which most predators leave alone
options.feedback: Ants are aggressive and often bite or spray acid, so many predators avoid them on sight, and a spider that looks and moves like one is avoided too.

options.label: They lost the use of two legs to injury
options.feedback: The spider still has eight working legs; the front pair is lifted on purpose, not disabled.

options.label: Six legs let them run faster over sand
options.feedback: Running speed is not the goal here; the front legs are held up and waved, not used for extra push.

options.label: They are copying the movement of the wind in grass
options.feedback: The movement copies an ant's stride and antenna-waving, not wind or grass.

items.ok_line: Eight legs pretending to be six, plus a pair of fake antennae.
items.ko_line: Those legs are not walking; they are being waved on purpose, like a signal.
items.exp_text: Some jumping spiders lift their front pair of legs off the ground and wave them near the head, so the body reads as six legs plus a pair of antennae instead of eight legs and none. That is the shape and gait of an ant, an insect many predators avoid because it bites or sprays acid. Looking like an ant lets a soft, harmless spider borrow an ant's reputation for trouble.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the large eye-like circles on some moths' wings?

options.label: They startle or mislead a predator into attacking the wrong spot
options.feedback: A sudden flash of two large false eyes can startle an attacker into hesitating, and even if it does not flee, it often strikes at the eyespot instead of the moth's body.

options.label: They help the moth see in more directions
options.feedback: The eyespots are simple patches of colored scales with no nerves or lenses; the moth's real eyes are the small ones on its head.

options.label: They mark where the moth's poison glands are
options.feedback: Most moths with eyespots carry no poison at all; the pattern is a bluff, not a label.

options.label: They attract insects for the moth to eat
options.feedback: Moths with eyespots feed on nectar or not at all as adults; the pattern plays no part in catching food.

items.ok_line: Two spots of color doing the work of a real threat.
items.ko_line: The pattern only has to look like eyes to something else. It does not need to work like eyes at all.
items.exp_title: Fooling an attacker for just long enough
items.exp_text: Some moths keep large circular markings hidden under their forewings and flash them open only when touched or threatened, revealing what looks like the staring eyes of a much bigger animal. The sudden appearance startles a bird enough to make it hesitate or peck at the wing edge instead of the body. That instant of hesitation, or a torn wing instead of a fatal bite, is often enough for the moth to get away.

items.prompt: Why do some caterpillars have a mottled black and white pattern that makes them look wet and lumpy?

options.label: The pattern makes them resemble bird droppings, which predators ignore
options.feedback: A bird searching leaves for food has no interest in another bird's droppings, so a caterpillar shaped and colored like one is passed over without a second look.

options.label: The pattern helps them absorb more sunlight
options.feedback: The dark and pale patches are placed for the disguise, not arranged for warmth.

options.label: It signals to other caterpillars that a leaf is already taken
options.feedback: Caterpillars have no way to read a pattern on another caterpillar as a claim on a leaf.

options.label: It washes off in rain to reveal warning colors underneath
options.feedback: Nothing changes after rain; the same mottled pattern is the disguise itself, not a coating over something else.

items.ok_line: Nothing eats a bird dropping on purpose.
items.ko_line: The pattern is not meant to attract or signal anything. It is meant to be dismissed at a glance.
items.exp_title: Disguised as something no one wants
items.exp_text: Rather than blend into a leaf's green, some caterpillars copy the blotchy black, white, and glossy look of fresh bird droppings, often curling their body to complete the shape. Birds hunt by sight and have no reason to peck at what looks like waste, so they scan straight past it while hunting for real prey. The caterpillar survives not by hiding, but by looking like something worthless.

items.prompt: Why does an orchid mantis, colored and shaped like a flower, sit among real blossoms?

options.label: It lures insects that come looking for nectar, then seizes them
options.feedback: Bees and flies land on it expecting a real bloom, and by the time they notice the mistake, the mantis's front legs have already closed on them.

options.label: It hides from predators until the flower dies
options.feedback: The mantis is not concealed at all; it sits in the open where insects are most likely to visit, which only makes sense if the goal is to be found.

options.label: The color helps it stay cool in the sun
options.feedback: Pale coloring has no special cooling effect here; the color's job is to match nearby petals, not manage temperature.

options.label: It feeds on the flower's petals directly
options.feedback: A mantis is a predator of other insects and does not eat plant material.

items.ok_line: A disguise built to attract, not to disappear.
items.ko_line: This disguise is not for hiding from something. It is for luring something in.
items.exp_title: A flower that catches what visits it
items.exp_text: An orchid mantis has pale, petal-shaped limbs and a body colored to match the blossoms growing around it, and it waits motionless among them rather than staying out of sight. Bees and flies searching for nectar are drawn straight to it, mistaking the mantis for another flower to visit. When one lands close enough, the mantis's front legs snap forward and grip it before it can react.

items.prompt: How does a speckled gray moth resting on tree bark avoid being eaten by day?

options.label: Its mottled pattern matches the bark's texture and color, breaking up its outline
options.feedback: Random flecks of gray, white, and black across the wings mirror the rough, blotchy look of bark closely enough that the moth's edges stop reading as an insect shape.

options.label: It only lands on bark that matches its exact shade after searching
options.feedback: The moth does not test or choose bark by matching; the same fixed pattern works across a range of similar-looking bark.

options.label: It flattens itself so no shadow is cast
options.feedback: Wing pattern, not flatness, is what does the hiding; the moth still casts a shadow like any resting insect.

options.label: It releases bark-scented chemicals to mask its smell
options.feedback: Most birds hunt these moths by sight, not smell, so a scent trick would not address the actual danger.

items.ok_line: The moth is still there in plain sight, just unreadable.
items.ko_line: The moth does not do anything active once it lands. Its wings are already doing the work before it even chooses a spot.
items.exp_title: A pattern that breaks up an outline
items.exp_text: A speckled gray moth's wings carry an irregular scatter of light and dark flecks that closely echoes the blotched, uneven look of bark and lichen. Resting flat against a trunk with wings folded, the moth's own outline stops standing out as a solid shape against the background. Birds hunting by sight scan right past a pattern that no longer separates itself from the bark around it.

items.prompt: How does a crab spider capture insects while sitting in the open on a flower?

options.label: It gradually shifts its color to match the flower and waits there, unnoticed, until prey lands
options.feedback: Pigment in the spider's body shifts over a few days to match white, yellow, or pink flowers, and it stays still on the bloom until an insect comes close enough to grab.

options.label: It spins a sticky web across the flower's petals
options.feedback: A crab spider builds no web at all; it relies entirely on ambush rather than a trap of silk.

options.label: It digs a burrow beneath the flower's roots
options.feedback: It waits above ground on the flower itself, in full view, not below in a burrow.

options.label: It chases insects down after spotting them from a distance
options.feedback: It waits motionless rather than pursuing; chasing prey across open air is not how it hunts.

items.ok_line: The same color as its trap and its cover.
items.ko_line: This spider hunts by disappearing into the very spot where prey is heading, not by trapping or pursuing it.
items.exp_title: Waiting the color of the flower
items.exp_text: A crab spider can slowly change its color over several days to match the petals of the flower it sits on, shifting toward white, yellow, or pink as needed. It does not spin a web or chase anything; it grips the bloom and stays still, matching its background so closely that arriving bees and flies fail to notice it. By the time an insect lands close enough to feed, the spider is already within reach and seizes it.
